evidence.snippet: Agentic AI refers to advanced artificial intelligence systems that can act autonomously to achieve a specific goal with minimal human intervention. Unlike traditional AI that only generates content or analyses data, agentic AI can reason, plan multistep actions, and execute tasks. In Salesforce, agentic AI — part of our Agentforce technology — is used to: • Automate complex workflows like lead qualification or service case resolution • Predict business outcomes, such as which deals are likely to close • Personalise every customer interaction across marketing, sales, and service channels

historical_reviews.notes: The official HubSpot documentation explicitly states that OAuth uses authorization tokens to connect an app to a HubSpot account. Apps intended for installation by multiple HubSpot accounts or listing on the HubSpot Marketplace must use OAuth. The flow exchanges an authorization code using the app's client ID and client secret for an access token and refresh token, and the access token is then used to authenticate API calls. This page supports OAuth2 as an authentication method for HubSpot's developer API.

evidence.snippet: OAuth is a secure means of authentication that uses authorization tokens rather than a password to connect your app to a user account. Initiating OAuth access is the first step towards allowing users to install your app in their HubSpot accounts.
evidence.heading: Documentation Index

evidence.snippet: For optimal security, all apps must use HubSpot’s OAuth protocol directly, or use your app’s static auth token if you’re building an app installed in a single account . Apps are responsible for storing time-to-live (TTL) data and refreshing user access tokens in accordance with this protocol. When an access token is generated, it will include an expires_in parameter indicating how long it can be used to make API calls before refreshing. Unauthorized (401) requests are not a valid indicator that a new access token must be retrieved.
evidence.heading: Authentication and security

evidence.snippet: 1) crm.objects.users.read lets an app hit the User Details API , which surfaces every user’s profile and team info; HubSpot treats that as sensitive, so only Super Admins (or users that have the full Add and edit users / Account access privilege, which is effectively the same in the permission model) can grant it — standard users, even with broad CRM rights, will hit an “insufficient permissions” error during the OAuth screen ( HubSpot Community ). 2) Giving a non‑admin the Add and edit users toggle under Settings › Users & Teams promotes them to an admin‑level role and is the only way HubSpot will let that user approve the scope ( HubSpot Knowledge Base ). 3) There’s no lighter “view‑only users” permission today, so if you want the install flow to work for regular users you have two options: a) drop the scope entirely and use a different endpoint (for example, Owners API) or b) flag it as an optional scope in the dev portal; then non‑admins can finish OAuth, but calls to /crm/v3/objects/users will 403 unless the installer was a Super Admin ( HubSpot Developers ). 4) If your app only needs to know which user installed it or to look up the current owner of a record, swap to crm.objects.owners.read (same restriction) or query the OAuth token metadata (/oauth/v1/access-tokens/{token}) instead, which returns the installer’s user and user_id without extra scopes. 5) Bottom line: to unblock testing, have a Super Admin install the app, or upgrade the tester’s permissions; for production, decide whether you truly need the full users object or can live with lighter data so non‑admin customers can connect without elevating their rights. Hope it helps.

evidence.snippet: OAuth is a secure means of authentication that uses authorization tokens rather than a password to connect your app to a user account. Initiating OAuth access is the first step towards allowing users to install your app in their HubSpot accounts.
evidence.heading: Documentation Index

evidence.snippet: Parameter Description How to use client_id An ID that serves as a unique identifier for your app. Get this from your app’s Auth settings page (as described above). redirect_uri The URL visitors will be redirected to after granting access to your app. You’ll also designate this on your app’s Auth settings page. Note: For security reasons, this URL must use https in production. (When testing using localhost , http can be used.) You also must use a domain, as IP addresses are not supported. scope A space-separated set of permissions that your app needs access to. Any scopes that you’ve checked off in your app’s Auth settings will be treated as required, and you’ll need to include them in this parameter or the authorization page will display an error. Additionally, users will get an error if they try to install your app in an account that doesn’t have access to an included scope. Consult the scopes reference documentation for more details about which endpoints can be accessed by specific scopes.
evidence.heading: Query parameters

evidence.snippet: Create a new app . After creating the app, you’ll be able to find the app’s client ID and client secret on the Auth page of your app settings .
evidence.heading: Set up OAuth authentication

evidence.snippet: Your app’s client secret will be used in step 4 below, after the user is redirected back to your app and you’re ready to generate the initial access and refresh tokens.
evidence.heading: Set up OAuth authentication

evidence.snippet: Use the client ID along with the query parameters and scopes outlined below in steps 2 and 3, to build your authorization URL.
evidence.heading: Set up OAuth authentication

evidence.snippet: OAuth requires you to set scopes, or permissions, for your app. Each scope provides access to a set of HubSpot API endpoints and allows users to grant your app access to specific tools in their HubSpot account. You can review your app’s current scopes in the development settings in your HubSpot account:
evidence.heading: Configure scopes

evidence.snippet: Click the Auth tab, then review your app’s required, conditionally required, and optional scopes in the Scopes section.
evidence.heading: Configure scopes

evidence.snippet: To update your app’s scopes, edit the corresponding scopes within the auth property of your app’s app-hsmeta.json file locally, then run the hs project upload command to upload the changes to your account.
evidence.heading: Configure scopes

evidence.snippet: Parameter How to use Description optional_scope A space-separated set of optional permissions for your app. Optional scopes will be automatically dropped from the authorization request if the user selects a HubSpot account that doesn’t have access to that tool (e.g., authorizing a Content Hub Enterprise scope in a HubSpot free account). If you’re using optional scopes, you will need to check the access token or refresh token to see which ones were granted. Check out the reference documentation on scopes for more details. state If this parameter is included in the authorization URL, the value will be included in a state query parameter when the user is directed to the redirect_uri . A string value that can be used to maintain the user’s state when they’re redirected back to your app.

evidence.snippet: 1) crm.objects.users.read lets an app hit the User Details API , which surfaces every user’s profile and team info; HubSpot treats that as sensitive, so only Super Admins (or users that have the full Add and edit users / Account access privilege, which is effectively the same in the permission model) can grant it — standard users, even with broad CRM rights, will hit an “insufficient permissions” error during the OAuth screen ( HubSpot Community ). 2) Giving a non‑admin the Add and edit users toggle under Settings › Users & Teams promotes them to an admin‑level role and is the only way HubSpot will let that user approve the scope ( HubSpot Knowledge Base ). 3) There’s no lighter “view‑only users” permission today, so if you want the install flow to work for regular users you have two options: a) drop the scope entirely and use a different endpoint (for example, Owners API) or b) flag it as an optional scope in the dev portal; then non‑admins can finish OAuth, but calls to /crm/v3/objects/users will 403 unless the installer was a Super Admin ( HubSpot Developers ). 4) If your app only needs to know which user installed it or to look up the current owner of a record, swap to crm.objects.owners.read (same restriction) or query the OAuth token metadata (/oauth/v1/access-tokens/{token}) instead, which returns the installer’s user and user_id without extra scopes. 5) Bottom line: to unblock testing, have a Super Admin install the app, or upgrade the tester’s permissions; for production, decide whether you truly need the full users object or can live with lighter data so non‑admin customers can connect without elevating their rights. Hope it helps.

The API is described as a RESTful API using JSON format, with OpenAPI 3 specifications available (d7:b58, d8:b120).

API tokens can be manually obtained from the Pipedrive app, with only one active token per user at a time, as explicitly documented (d0:b7, d0:b9, d0:b10).

evidence.heading: Pipedrive launches native MCP server, bringing CRM workflows directly into AI assistants

evidence.snippet: New York, June 30, 2026 – Pipedrive , the easy and intelligent CRM for small and medium-sized businesses, today announced the launch of its native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, enabling customers to securely connect Pipedrive with AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and other MCP-compatible tools.
evidence.heading: Pipedrive launches native MCP server, bringing CRM workflows directly into AI assistants

evidence.snippet: MCP is an open standard that enables AI assistants to securely connect to external tools and data sources. Through Pipedrive’s native MCP server, AI assistants can interact with live CRM data in real time while respecting existing user permissions and maintaining a full audit trail of actions performed.

evidence.snippet: This reference helps you implement the RESTful Pipedrive API. This API uses a JSON format for output and is capable of handling CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) requests. The API is stateless – all requests are validated against an API token. The API token can be obtained manually from the Pipedrive app.
evidence.heading: API Reference

evidence.snippet: Pipedrive is a sales CRM with an intuitive RESTful API , webhooks, app extensions and API clients to help you build an app for the Pipedrive Marketplace .

Pipedrive's API and extension points cover the majority of our core product's functionality. As our product is constantly growing, so is our API. To be up to date with new additions and updates, please check out and subscribe to our Changelog .
evidence.heading: API Reference > OpenAPI 3

evidence.snippet: You can click on the "Run in Postman" button below to interact with our API. We have a tutorial for using Pipedrive API in Postman or Insomnia, but if you prefer to use a different tool, you can always import our OpenAPI 3 specification files (available for both v1 and v2 APIs) into your tool of choice. See this article to learn more about Pipedrive API v2. Keep in mind that we'll occasionally update our OpenAPI 3 specification files, so you might need to re-import them from time to time. For ready-to-use SDKs, read below under "Client libraries".

evidence.snippet: There is no static API reference for Twenty. Each workspace has its own schema — when you add a custom object (say Invoice ), it immediately gets REST and GraphQL endpoints identical to built-in objects like Company or Person . The API is generated from the schema, so endpoints use your object and field names directly — no opaque IDs. Your workspace-specific API documentation is available under Settings → API & Webhooks after creating an API key. It includes an interactive playground where you can execute real calls against your data.
evidence.heading: Schema-per-tenant APIs

evidence.snippet: Core API — /rest/ and /graphql/ CRUD on records: People, Companies, Opportunities, your custom objects. Query, filter, traverse relations. Metadata API — /rest/metadata/ and /metadata/ Schema management: create/modify/delete objects, fields, and relations. This is how you programmatically change your data model. Both are available as REST and GraphQL. GraphQL adds batch upserts and the ability to traverse relations in a single query. Same underlying data either way.
evidence.heading: Two APIs

decisions.reason: The official product body passages describe Podio as a customizable work management platform enabling teams to collaborate, automate workflows, and integrate with other tools to streamline business processes, matching the stated fact.

The documentation passages show Podio supports multiple OAuth2 flows including app authentication flow, server-side flow, and username and password flow, not only 'oauth2' as a single method. The fact lists only 'oauth2' without specifying flows, but the passages indicate multiple OAuth2 flows and username/password flow as well, so the fact is incomplete and thus unsupported as stated.
The documentation provides detailed evidence of a documented API with multiple endpoints and authentication flows, supporting the fact that an API is available.

The documentation details multiple API areas grouped by functionality, including core areas (applications, comments, files, hooks, items, statuses, tasks) and other areas (linked accounts, grants, embeds, forms, notifications, questions, reminders, subscriptions, tags, users, views, widgets), supporting the stated breadth of the API.

The documentation supports the existence of a resource API, resource credentials, and onboarding processes, although integration has not been executed, supporting the fact that the product is buildable with documented constraints.
The rationale is directly supported by the documentation passages stating that the documentation supports a resource API, resource credentials, and onboarding, but integration has not been executed.

evidence.snippet: The app authentication flow is suitable in situations where you only need data from a single app and do not wish authenticate as a specific user. It is similar to the username & password flow , but uses the app ID and a special app token as the login credentials.
evidence.heading: Authentication > App authentication flow

evidence.snippet: When you authenticate as an app you can only access that specific app and if you create content it will appear as having been created by the app itself rather than a specific user. Good uses for the app authentication flow are automated scripts that run without any user interaction.
evidence.heading: Authentication > App authentication flow

evidence.snippet: The server-side flow works by sending your user to Podio to authorize. It's a four step process:
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: You redirect your user to Podio for authorization
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: Podio redirects back to your web app with an authorization code
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: You use the authorization code to obtain an access token
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: You use the access token for all API requests
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: The first step is to redirect your user to Podio's authorization endpoint, providing your client_id and a redirect_uri. The redirect_uri must be on the same domain as the domain you specified when you applied for your API Key. The endpoint you must redirect to is:
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: https://podio.com/oauth/authorize?client_id= YOUR_APP_ID &redirect_uri= YOUR_URL &scope= SCOPE_STRING
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: If the user is not logged in to Podio he will be asked to login. Then we will present a screen showing what the user is granting access to:
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: If the user for some reason denies access, the application is not authorized, and the OAuth flow will redirect the user back to the URL, passed in the redirect_uri parameter with these parameters:
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: After granting access the user will be redirected to the URL you passed in the redirect_uri parameter with an authorization code appended:
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: You must then use the authorization code to obtain an access token. To authenticate your app, you must pass the authorization code and your client_secret to our endpoint. In return you will receive an access token. Make a POST like this:
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: HTTP METHOD: POST URL: https://api.podio.com/oauth/token/v 2 HEADER: "Content-Type: application/json" BODY: { "grant_type" : "authorization_code" , "client_id" : YOUR_APP_ID , "redirect_uri" : YOUR_URL , "client_secret" : YOUR_APP_SECRET , "code" : THE_AUTHORIZATION_CODE , }
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: If your app is successfully authenticated and the authorization code from the user is valid, the API will return the access token:
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: { "access_token" : ACCESS_TOKEN , "token_type" : "bearer" , "expires_in" : EXPIRES_IN , "refresh_token" : REFRESH_TOKEN , "scope" : GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING , "ref" : { "type" : "user" , "id" : USER_ID } }
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

evidence.snippet: See Scopes & Permissions for details about the value of GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING
evidence.heading: Authentication > Server-side flow

decisions.reason: Multiple official product body passages describe Zoho CRM as a customizable AI-powered customer relationship management platform that helps businesses manage leads, sales, marketing, and customer data efficiently (d1:b2, d19:b2, d20:b15, d19:b54).
Documentation explicitly states that Zoho CRM API uses OAuth 2.0 protocol for authentication and that OAuth2.0 requests are authenticated with an access token passed as a bearer token (d0:b2, d4:b2).

Only REST API is explicitly documented with resource actions and usage (d14:b16). GraphQL is described as a query language available in certain editions but no actual API resource or endpoint documentation is provided, and GraphQL APIs are not available in trial versions (d17:b2, d17:b7, d17:b8). Thus, GraphQL API availability is not sufficiently documented as an API type.
Documented API resources and protocols exist with REST API endpoints and OAuth 2.0 authentication documented (d7:b2, d7:b5, d9:b3, d9:b4, d9:b6, d9:b5, d14:b16, d17:b2, d17:b7, d17:b8).

Documentation details specific API actions such as Roles API for retrieving roles data and Update Share Permissions API for updating, creating, and revoking share permissions on records (d7:b2, d7:b5, d9:b3, d9:b4, d9:b6, d9:b5).

Documentation explicitly states that developers can self-service create OAuth client credentials by registering their application in Zoho API console to obtain Client ID and Client Secret (d6:b8, d6:b10, d6:b11).

Documentation supports existence of resource API, resource credentials, and onboarding process with detailed API documentation and client registration steps, although integration has not been executed (d7:b2, d7:b5, d9:b3, d9:b4, d9:b6, d9:b5, d14:b16, d17:b2, d17:b7, d17:b8, d0:b2, d4:b2, d6:b8, d6:b10, d6:b11, d6:b2, d4:b22, d4:b24, d5:b54, d7:b33, d9:b61).

The rationale is directly supported by documentation stating that resource API, resource credentials, and onboarding are documented, though integration has not been executed (d7:b2, d7:b5, d9:b3, d9:b4, d9:b6, d9:b5, d14:b16, d17:b2, d17:b7, d17:b8, d0:b2, d4:b2, d6:b8, d6:b10, d6:b11, d6:b2, d4:b22, d4:b24, d5:b54, d7:b33, d9:b61).

evidence.snippet: Intelligent automation meets intuitive design. Built with AI at its core, Zoho CRM supercharges your business to get ahead without the overhead.
evidence.heading: The easiest AI CRM for growth.

evidence.snippet: Zoho CRM offers everything you need to increase leads, accelerate sales, and measure sales performance.
evidence.heading: Features that make selling easier

evidence.snippet: In its crudest form, CRM software helps you efficiently manage the information you've collected on your customers, as well as on prospects who might be interested in doing business with you. You can store and manage this data with a simple goal in mind: to enhance your business relationships by improving customer retention and customer acquisition. Coupled with the power of AI, a CRM can give you insights into customer behavior, the state of your sales pipeline, how each individual salesperson is performing, and much more.
evidence.heading: What is CRM? > What does CRM software do?

evidence.snippet: One CRM, and infinite ways to make it yours. Zoho CRM isn't just software—it's a canvas for your vision, a sandbox for testing, and a flexible framework for capturing data and grouping information. It equips you to design an environment that adapts to your unique workflows. It's the capable foundation your system rests upon—a system that was built entirely by you.
evidence.heading: Features that make selling easier > Customization without limits: Designed & defined by you

evidence.snippet: Make sure to give your new API key an informative name so that you’ll be able to easily tell which key is used for which integration. evidence.heading: API keys > Creating an API key

evidence.snippet: An API key is a secret token, which is used to authenticate your requests to the Close API. It should be kept private and stored securely. evidence.snippet: You should always store your API keys securely and you should never share them with parties you don’t trust. decisions.reason: The passage d11:b246 explicitly states that DealCloud is a flexible system of record used by many industries with unique schemas, custom objects, fields, and relationships, matching the claimed purpose.
Passages d7:b250 and d5:b276 show usage of API keys and bearer tokens for authorization, supporting the claim that 'api_key' and 'bearer_token' are used as authentication methods.
Passages d0:b246 and d8:b250 show REST API endpoints and usage, supporting the claim that the API type is REST.
Multiple passages (d0:b246 through d0:b265, d8:b250, d5:b276, d11:b249, d4:b261, d7:b247, d2:b224) document API endpoints and usage, supporting that the API is available.

Passages d8:b250, d5:b276, d11:b249, d4:b261, d7:b247, and d2:b224 describe API endpoints for reading data, schema, user info, publication topics, updating records, managing user proxy assignments and group permissions, and deleting users from groups, supporting the claimed breadth.

Passages d7:b250 and d7:b247 describe that users can self-service create API keys if enabled in their profile and that enabling API access requires user group permissions and possibly admin or CSM assistance, supporting the access model claim with caveats.
Passage d9:b256 states a default DealCloud MCP Server is available out-of-the-box, supporting the claim that MCP is available.
Passage d3:b243 states that the DealCloud MCP Server is provided by DealCloud as a native MCP surface, supporting the claim.
Passage d3:b243 explicitly states that the DealCloud MCP Server is owned and operated by DealCloud, supporting the claim.
Passages d3:b243, d9:b256, and d9:b258 provide detailed notes on MCP server availability, ownership, provider, and limitations, supporting the claim.

Passages d0:b246 through d0:b265, d8:b250, d5:b276, d11:b249, d4:b261, d7:b247, d2:b224, d7:b250, d5:b254, d4:b260, and d5:b271 provide documentation supporting resource API, credentials, and onboarding, supporting buildability with documented constraints.
The same passages as for buildability support the rationale that documentation supports resource API, credentials, and onboarding, though integration has not been executed.

Passages d7:b247, d4:b260, and d4:b261 document that enabling API access requires user group permissions and that user proxy assignments must be configured to authorize proxied API calls, supporting the primary blockers claim.

evidence.snippet: DealCloud is a flexible system of record used by many industries. Because each industry may use different object models and terminology, DealCloud does not use a fixed schema. Instead, every DealCloud site can have its own unique schema, with custom objects, fields, names, and relationships.

evidence.snippet: #!/usr/bin/env ruby # # This code snippet shows how to enable SSL in Sinatra+Thin. # require 'sinatra' require 'thin' require 'json' require 'slim' require 'json' require "net/http" require "uri" class MyThinBackend < :: Thin :: Backends :: TcpServer def initialize ( host , port , options ) super (host, port) @ssl = true @ssl_options = options end end configure do set :environment , :production set :bind , '0.0.0.0' #:set :port, 443 set :server , "thin" class << settings def server_settings { :backend => MyThinBackend , :private_key_file => File . dirname ( __FILE__ ) + "/pkey.pem" , :cert_chain_file => File . dirname ( __FILE__ ) + "/cert.crt" , :verify_peer => false } end end end get '/' do File . read ( 'intercom.html' ) end get '/home' do "Welcome Back" end get '/callback' do #Get the Code passed back to our redirect callback @code = params[ :code ] @state = params[ :state ] puts "CODE: #{ @code } " puts "STATE: #{ @state } " #We can do a Post now to get the access token uri = URI . parse ( "https://api.intercom.io/auth/eagle/token" ) response = Net :: HTTP . post_form (uri, { "code" => params[ :code ], "client_id" => "XXXXXXXXXXXXX" , "client_secret" => "YYYYYYYYYYYY" }) #Break Up the response and print out the Access Token rsp = JSON . parse (response. body ) puts "ACCESS TOKEN: #{rsp[ "token" ]} " redirect '/home' end post '/callback' do push = JSON . parse (request. body . read ) puts "I got some JSON: #{push. inspect } " end

evidence.snippet: Our REST API is a core building block of the Intercom Platform. You can use it to retrieve and update information from your own Intercom account, or to integrate Intercom into your own product. It's completely up to you and your custom use case.
evidence.heading: About our REST API

evidence.snippet: Intercom workspaces can be hosted in three distinct regions - US, EU and Australia. If you call api.intercom.io , we'll attempt to route your request to the correct region, but if you would prefer to specify the region where you expect the data to be stored, you can do so using the endpoints below. These replace the start of the URIs for each REST API endpoint, to connect to the specific regions. For example, to call the /me endpoint for a workspace stored in the EU, you would call https://api.eu.intercom.io/me instead of https://api.intercom.io/me .
evidence.heading: About our REST API > Regional Hosting

evidence.snippet: Regional Hosting Location REST Endpoint to use US https://api.intercom.io/ Europe https://api.eu.intercom.io Australia https://api.au.intercom.io
evidence.heading: About our REST API > Regional Hosting

evidence.snippet: The API uses common approaches for the following:
evidence.heading: About our REST API > Common Approaches

evidence.snippet: Function Description Data API data is JSON encoded with UTF-8. API JSON is either a single object or a list of objects. Errors 4xx and 5xx responses returning JSON with error codes. Rate Limiting Controls how many requests can be made in a time window. HTTP Methods are used in accordance with HTTP (GET POST and DELETE are the primary methods used) and resources are identified using URIs. All API requests are sent over HTTPS.

    * **Read** for retrieving resource information.
    * **Write** for creating and updating resources.

It appears like Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the protocol that everyone is moving towards as it puts the burden of keeping everything “tidy” on the service provider rather than the client. There are already many official MCP servers available and more on the way. There are also community developed ones.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI applications securely connect to external data sources and tools. With the Front MCP server, AI-powered tools like Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, and others can interact directly with your Front account and API documentation using natural language — no manual API calls required.

evidence.snippet: Authentication and security. Plain uses Machine Users — dedicated API identities for bots and automations, separate from human user accounts. Each Machine User supports multiple API keys with fine-grained permission scopes ( customer:read , thread:create , label:create , and more), so you can grant an integration exactly the access it needs and nothing more. Multiple keys per Machine User means you can rotate credentials without downtime. Webhook verification uses HMAC-SHA256 request signing, and Plain supports mTLS (mutual TLS) for both webhooks and Customer Cards — the platform authenticates your server, and your server authenticates Plain. SOC 2 Type II certified.

evidence.snippet: GraphQL API. Plain's API endpoint ( core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1 ) exposes the full schema at /schema.graphql , which means you can auto-generate typed clients in any language — not just TypeScript. Pagination follows the Relay specification: cursor-based, supports both forward and backward traversal, with up to 100 results per page. Mutation errors are structured with field-level detail and typed as VALIDATION, FORBIDDEN, or INTERNAL, so your code can handle failures precisely instead of parsing error strings. Plain also ships a built-in API Explorer at app.plain.com/developer/api-explorer for testing queries against live data without leaving the browser.

historical_reviews.notes: Aircall's official Public API documentation explicitly supports two authentication methods: OAuth 2.0 and HTTP Basic Authentication. OAuth is intended for apps built for multiple Aircall companies and marketplace integrations. Basic Authentication is intended for Aircall customers building for their own account, using api_id as the username and api_token as the password. OAuth access tokens are used as Bearer tokens.

historical_reviews.what_to_verify: Can a developer obtain API access directly, or is payment, admin, partner or sales approval required?
historical_reviews.correction_reason: Aircall API access is permission-gated at the company level. Integrations can only be enabled or installed by an Aircall Admin. Existing Aircall customers can create Basic Auth credentials for their own company from Company Settings > API Keys. For public or multi-company integrations, Aircall requires OAuth, and developers must obtain client_id and client_secret from Aircall after submitting the partner/OAuth setup form. Marketplace listing also requires OAuth. The inspected source does not establish a universal paid-plan gate for ordinary API access, so admin_approval is the best overall access-model classification, with additional partner approval/provisioning for public integrations.

historical_reviews.what_to_verify: What concrete restriction blocks integration, if any? Absence of evidence is not proof of no blocker.
historical_reviews.correction_reason: Shopify integration access depends on the app's distribution model and requested data. Custom-distribution apps can be installed on a specific store, or multiple stores within the same Shopify Plus organization, without Shopify app approval. Public-distribution apps intended for multiple merchants require Shopify approval through App Review before App Store distribution. Access is also scope-based, and certain sensitive capabilities require additional permission or Shopify approval, including protected customer data and restricted scopes. Therefore Shopify is buildable, but broad/public integrations are conditioned by review and permission requirements rather than a universal access block.

historical_reviews.correction_reason: Shopify's GraphQL Admin API authenticates requests with an access token sent in the X-Shopify-Access-Token header. Shopify documents OAuth, usually token exchange or the authorization code grant depending on app type, as the standard flow for obtaining that token when an app acts on behalf of a merchant. Therefore OAuth2 is the authorization/token-acquisition mechanism, while the issued bearer-style access token authenticates individual API requests.

historical_reviews.source_candidate_note: Stage02 official attribution/seed; Uday must confirm product identity and ownership. Candidate may not support this field.
historical_reviews.what_to_verify: Can a developer obtain API access directly, or is payment, admin, partner or sales approval required?
historical_reviews.correction_reason: Ramp supports different access paths depending on the integration model. Existing Ramp customers can create credentials for internal integrations, while server-to-server integrations use the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials flow. Third-party or public integrations must use the Authorization Code flow, and the Ramp user granting access must have Developer API authorization permissions, typically an Admin or Business Owner. Partner integrations intended for other businesses follow Ramp's partner process: developers build and test in Sandbox, apply for production access, and Ramp reviews the integration before production approval. Sandbox access itself is also requested through a form. Therefore ordinary production integration access is conditioned by account/admin permissions, with additional Ramp approval for public partner integrations, rather than being universally self-service.

historical_reviews.what_to_verify: What concrete restriction blocks integration, if any? Absence of evidence is not proof of no blocker.
historical_reviews.correction_reason: Consensus does expose both an MCP server and an API, so integration is not technically blocked. However, access is commercially conditioned. The documentation states that API-key gateway credentials map to the Enterprise tier, while paid plans provide defined request limits and paper limits. Some enterprise-specific setups, such as confidential OAuth clients for gateways that cannot use Dynamic Client Registration, require contacting sales for manual provisioning. Therefore the practical blocker is not lack of API/MCP capability, but paid/Enterprise access requirements and, for some gateway configurations, sales-assisted credential provisioning.
